title: Make It Move
tagline: Your first physical computer reacts to you.
objectives: I can explain the difference between an input and an output using real examples.
I can build a working program on a real micro:bit that reacts to an input.
I can test my program and use what happens (or doesn't) to find and fix problems myself.

config.headline: Today you make a computer react.
lines: In this lesson you will learn what an INPUT and an OUTPUT are — and you will prove you know, by building a tiny computer that reacts when you press it.

Look at the three photos below. A lift button, a pedestrian crossing, a fitness tracker: something happens (the INPUT — a press, a step), and something reacts (the OUTPUT — the doors open, the green man lights, the step count goes up). Every machine you have ever used works on that one idea.

The computer in your hands today is called a micro:bit — a computer the size of a biscuit, with two buttons and a grid of 25 tiny lights. You will work in a pair with the person sitting beside you, one micro:bit between the two of you, and together you will TELL it how to react: press a button, get a picture; shake it, get a ghost.

By the end of the hour you will have built a program on a real device, tested it with your own hands, and learned the first rule of every programmer's life: when it doesn't work, the code is trying to tell you something.

config.title: The Signal Relay Ladder
config.intro:
This is where you learn to BUILD, and you do it with the person beside you: one micro:bit shared between the two of you. The ladder has four small challenges, called rungs, and you climb them in order. Rung 1 needs no computer at all. Rungs 2, 3 and 4 are real programs you build in MakeCode, copy onto the micro:bit, and test with your own hands.

You BOTH build every rung, each on your OWN computer. Talk it through together as you go, and try it on the simulator on your own screen first — that is the little micro:bit picture in the corner of MakeCode. You share the real micro:bit for the real test, so take turns: at each rung, one of you copies the program across and presses the button while the other watches. Swap over at every rung, so you both do both.

Nobody marks this. The micro:bit itself is the judge — either it does what the card says, or it doesn't, and you can both see which.

unplugged.title: Rung 1 — The Human Circuit
lines: This first rung needs no computer at all: you and the person beside you are going to BE the machine. Stand up.

Every machine from the start of the lesson — the lift, the crossing, the step-counter — has a part that NOTICES something happen (computing calls it a SENSOR) and a part that REACTS (an ACTUATOR). Decide now: one of you is the sensor, the other is the actuator.
SENSOR: mime pressing an invisible button. ACTUATOR: the instant you see the press, throw both arms up — you are REACTING, like the heart appearing on the screen after button A was pressed.
New signal! SENSOR: mime shaking the micro:bit. ACTUATOR: wave both hands — you are REACTING again, but this time to a completely different signal. Same rule, new trigger: when THIS happens, do THAT.
Swap jobs and run both signals again, so each of you has played both parts.

Finish by saying it out loud together (or a loud whisper will do if you prefer — or you could make a rap out of it (joking — but feel free to try!)): the press is the INPUT. The reaction is the OUTPUT. The rule connecting them — when THIS happens, do THAT — is an EVENT. Those three words run the whole hour.
unplugged.confirm: We both played Sensor and Actuator — and said the magic sentence
soloLines: This first rung needs no computer at all — and no partner on a catch-up: YOU are the whole machine, both parts of it.
Every machine from the start of the lesson has a part that NOTICES something happen (a SENSOR) and a part that REACTS (an ACTUATOR). Today you play both.
With one hand, mime pressing an invisible button. The instant you do, throw your other arm up — that's the heart appearing on the screen.
New signal: mime shaking a device with one hand, and wave the other — that's the message scrolling across.

Finish by saying it out loud (quietly counts): the press is the INPUT. The reaction is the OUTPUT. The rule connecting them — when THIS happens, do THAT — is an EVENT. Those three words run the whole hour.
unplugged.soloConfirm: I ran both signals — and said the magic sentence

rungs.title: Rung 2 — Your First Signal
rungs.target: Your challenge: make the micro:bit show a HAPPY FACE whenever button B is pressed. You built the button A one together with the film — this one is yours, on a different button, with a different picture.
rungs.test: Copy your program onto the micro:bit: press Download in MakeCode, then drag the downloaded file onto the MICROBIT drive. Copying it across like this is called FLASHING the program onto the device — that is the word your teacher will use. The film button below replays exactly how, if you need it. Then press the real button B. Did the happy face appear? (If your device won't connect, the on-screen simulator counts while your teacher sorts it.)
rungs.hint: Start from the same shape you saw in the film: an 'on button pressed' block with a 'show icon' block INSIDE it. Then change the dropdown on the event block from A to B, and pick the happy face in the icon dropdown. A block floating on its own never runs.

rungs.title: Rung 3 — A Different Kind of Signal
rungs.target: Your challenge: a button is not the only way to talk to a micro:bit. Make a GHOST appear when the micro:bit is SHAKEN. Leave your button A and button B blocks exactly where they are — this is a third signal, added alongside them.
rungs.test: Copy your program onto the micro:bit: press Download in MakeCode, then drag the downloaded file onto the MICROBIT drive. Copying it across like this is called FLASHING the program onto the device — that is the word your teacher will use. The film button below replays exactly how, if you need it. Then give it a real shake. Does the ghost appear? Now press A and B again to check they still work — all three signals live in the same program.
rungs.hint: You need an 'on shake' block, not an 'on button pressed' one — look for it in the Input drawer. Put a 'show icon' block inside it and choose the ghost, the shape pictured on the card.
rungs.imgAlt: The ghost icon as it appears on the micro:bit: a five by five pattern of lit LEDs shaped like a ghost
rungs.imgCap: THIS is the ghost. Look for this shape in the icon dropdown — it is easy to miss.

rungs.title: Rung 4 — The Vanishing Ghost
rungs.target: Your challenge: your ghost turns up and never leaves. Make it vanish on its own. When the micro:bit is SHAKEN, this is what should happen: 1. the GHOST appears — 2. it stays on screen for one second — 3. the screen clears itself.
rungs.test: Copy it across and give it a real shake. Does the ghost appear, hold, then vanish cleanly — every single time? Now prove the pause is earning its place: take the pause block out, copy the program across again, and shake. The ghost seems never to appear at all — the clear wipes it before your eyes can catch it. Put the pause back.
rungs.hint: The ORDER inside 'on shake' matters: show icon, THEN pause (ms) 1000, THEN clear screen. The pause is the only thing giving the ghost time on screen — without it, 'clear screen' wipes it before your eyes can catch it and you see nothing at all. (Your button A heart stayed put because nothing came along to clear it.)

stretch.title: Stretch — Two Buttons at Once
stretch.target: Your stretch challenge: see if you can make one input trigger a whole SEQUENCE. When A and B are pressed at the SAME TIME, this is what should happen: 1. a heart appears — 2. it holds for half a second — 3. a happy face takes its place.
stretch.test: Copy it across and press A + B together on the real device. Heart, half-second pause, then happy face — every single time?

config.introSolo: This is where you learn to BUILD — on your own today, so you play both parts yourself. The ladder has four small challenges, called rungs, and you climb them in order. Each rung card tells you exactly what your program should do: build it in MakeCode (in your other tab, or the on-screen simulator), then run the real test yourself. Nobody marks this — the micro:bit is still the judge.
config.help: Read the rung card, build what it asks for in MakeCode (its own tab), then TEST it for real — press the button, do the shake. If it worked, press the gold button and the next rung appears. Stuck? That's what the Debug Hint is for — it costs 2 XP and nudges you toward the fix without giving it away. The film button replays the MakeCode film without losing your place.
config.setupLead: Before you start rung 2, set MakeCode up like this:
setup: Open MakeCode using the button above. Keep it in its own tab all lesson.

Build each rung (each activity) in the SAME project that you created for the video tutorial you've just completed on the previous screen, which you called make-it-move. The project name stays the same as you climb the ladder and complete each new activity — you never start a new one.

Every time you press Download it saves a new copy of the WHOLE project, replacing the one from last time. If a box asks whether you want to replace the old file, say yes — that is exactly what you want.

config.title: Bank your build
config.intro: A build that lives on one computer is a build you can lose. In this step you learn the habit that protects every piece of work you ever make in DT: save it to your Google Drive — the Vault from Lesson 1 — and it follows your login to ANY machine, even at home. The website will then genuinely check your Drive and only give the badge when the file is really there.

steps.title: Download your build
steps.text: In MakeCode press the purple Download button. A file ending in .hex lands in the computer's Downloads folder — that file IS your program.

steps.title: Open your Vault
steps.text: New tab → drive.google.com → open School → DT Work. Don't see those folders? Click + New → Folder, make 'School', open it, make 'DT Work' inside — thirty seconds, then carry on.

steps.title: Drag it in
steps.text: Drag the .hex file from Downloads into DT Work. Done — the website can now verify it's really there.

config.passText: Your build now follows your login anywhere — that's the whole point of the Vault. Next lesson you can pick up exactly where you left off, on any machine.
config.failText: Not there yet. Check each step above — especially that the file went INTO the DT Work folder, not just onto the desktop — then run the inspection again.
config.help: Three steps: download your program from MakeCode, open your Google Drive in a new tab, drag the file into School → DT Work. Then press the inspection button and the website checks your Drive for real. If it says the file isn't there, check it went INSIDE the DT Work folder, not just onto the desktop.

demo.note: The program saved in the film is just an example — do not copy it. You are saving your own program, make-it-move.hex.

config.intro: Two scenarios before you go — and unlike everything else today, these ARE marked: your teacher sees how the class did, so think like a debugger before you answer.

items.stem:
Let's say you've built a program from the following instructions:
`on button A pressed → show heart`
You press button A on the micro:bit but nothing appears. What is the MOST likely reason?
options: You forgot to flash the code onto the micro:bit
Button A only works if you press button B at the same time

items.stem:
Here is what your finished program does:
`press button A → a heart appears on the LED grid`
Which part of that is the INPUT?

config.help: Two marked questions about today. Answer on your own — your teacher sees how the class did. Your verdicts arrive once the whole report is filed, at the end of the last screen.

config.intro: Last one: four real blocks, one working program. Put them in the order that matches the sentence — you spent today learning why order inside an event matters.

item.prompt: When you shake it, a ghost appears on the screen, holds for one second, then the screen clears.

config.help: Click blocks from the tray into your program, in the order the sentence describes. Check when you're sure — you'll be shown the working order if it's off.

config.intro: Two last jobs, so the micro:bits are ready for the next class.

steps.title: Clear your program off the micro:bit
steps.text: Your program is still sitting on the micro:bit, and it would still be there for the next class — they would press a button and see YOUR heart appear. Holding the reset button cannot remove it; the only way to clear a micro:bit is to send it a different program. So you are going to send it an empty one.
lines: Click the button below. A file called clear-my-microbit.hex lands in your Downloads folder.
Drag that file onto the MICROBIT drive, exactly the way you have done all lesson.
The yellow light on the micro:bit flashes while the file copies across. When it stops, the micro:bit is empty.
Check it: press button A and button B. Nothing happens now — and that is exactly right.
steps.note: Nothing you made today is lost. Your program is saved in MakeCode and in your Drive from Bank Your Build — this only clears the micro:bit itself.
steps.confirm: My micro:bit is empty — A and B do nothing

steps.title: Switch your micro:bit off
steps.text: Your micro:bit has a small black button on the BACK. It is called the reset button, and holding it down switches the micro:bit off so your program stops running. Here is what to do:
lines: Turn your micro:bit over so you are looking at the back. Find the small black button — the picture below shows you exactly where it is.
Press and HOLD that button for about 5 seconds.

Watch the tiny red light on the back. It fades from bright red to nothing — that is how you know your program has stopped. (If the USB lead is still plugged in, the light may then blink slowly. That is normal: it just means the computer is still feeding it power. It stays off once you unplug the lead.)
Let go, unplug the USB lead, and hand your micro:bit back to your teacher.
steps.imgAlt: The back of a micro:bit V2. The small black reset button is circled near the top edge, sitting between the silver USB socket and the white battery socket.
steps.imgCap: The reset button is on the BACK, between the USB socket and the battery socket. Photo: SimonWaldherr, CC BY 4.0, annotated by us.
steps.note: Nothing you built today is lost. Your program is saved in MakeCode, and in your Drive from Bank Your Build — it was only the micro:bit itself you cleared in the job above. Holding this button switches the micro:bit off; it never deletes anything of yours.
steps.confirm: My micro:bit is switched off and handed back

config.help: Two jobs. First, clear your program off the micro:bit: click the button on the card to get the empty program, then drag it onto the MICROBIT drive just like you have all lesson — when the yellow light stops flashing, press A and B and nothing should happen. Then hold the small black button on the back for about 5 seconds until the little red light fades, unplug the USB lead and hand it back. Nothing you made is lost: your work is in MakeCode and in your Drive.

statements: I can tell the difference between an input and an output.
I can build code that reacts when something happens.
I can test my code and notice when it's not working.
